It’s a different kind of satisfaction when you understand why something works instead of just getting it to work.



I think this is one of the best ways you can use AI while learning software engineering.



When I was learning to code, I would have loved a tool that could look at a compiler error, explain what it meant, and then let me fix it myself.



Quite different from saying, "Claude, fix this."



Because when you write the code yourself, struggle with it, and finally understand why it works, you build instincts that stay with you much longer.



And those instincts help you during you career.



They show up when production breaks, when AI gives you code that looks correct but is subtly wrong.



They also show up when two solutions both work, but one of them is going to create a nightmare six months later.



This is where I think a lot of young developers are getting stuck now.



AI has become so deeply embedded in the workflow that some people have not written good code by hand in months.



The moment they try to go back, there is anxiety.



"What if I am slower now?"

"What if I forgot the syntax?"

"What if I cannot solve this without help?"



That is a genuine feeling.



And I do not think the answer is to stop using AI.



The better balance is:

→ Use AI to explain the error

→ Ask it why the bug happened

→ Ask for hints before solutions

→ Compare your approach with its approach

→ Make it challenge your assumptions

→ Let it review what you wrote after you finish



For learning, this is incredibly powerful.



You still get the speed and access of AI, but the actual thinking stays with you.



And later, when you are working professionally with agents all day, that foundation becomes the thing that lets you judge their output instead of blindly trusting it.



AI can help you get unstuck. Don’t let it skip the part where your brain actually learns why the system works, especially when you’re learning.



I’m not writing code by hand now, but I’ve written enough to understand, and at times I’ll just fix the errors myself instead of spinning up an agent. That feeling still hits different, haha.
